newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Future HK leader backs China call for more troops.
newsitem.headline: Future HK leader backs China call for more troops.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader on Sunday backed China's demand to allow more People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops into the territory before Britain hands the territory to back China on July 1.
Hong Kong chief executive designate Tung Chee-hwa told reporters that China's demand made sense.
"It is a good thing if they can arrive early to take up their duties," Tung told local television news.
"The PLA's arrival symbolises the change of sovereignty. Their discipline is very good, in fact they're an outstanding group," he said.
An advance party of 196 PLA soldiers is already in Hong Kong setting up facilities for the eventual military garrison that will be stationed in Hong Kong.

Media reports have said Beijing wants to send about 2,000 troops to Hong Kong on the afternoon of June 30 so that the garrison can take up its duties from the moment that sovereignty transfers to China at midnight on that day.
But London has insisted there is no need for more troops before the handover.
Outgoing Hong Kong governor Chris Patten on Saturday praised the behaviour of the PLA advance guard and said he was sure there would be a "resolution" over the additional deployment.

"We obviously want to ensure that the Chinese garrison arrives in the most efficient way, so we are continuing to talk about how the arrival of the rest of the garrison can be managed and handled," Patten said.

Senior Chinese officials have said that PLA troops need to enter the territory earlier than July 1 to ensure security for Chinese President Jiang Zemin, who is attending handover celebrations in Hong Kong.
China has given no figure for the number of troops it plans eventually to station in Hong Kong. At the height of British rule, London maintained about 10,000 troops in the colony.
Some of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people are wary of a PLA presence because of memories of how the troops put down the pro-democracy movement in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.
Earlier this week, a mini-row broke out over allegations of special customs treatment for PLA troops already in Hong Kong.
However, both Chinese and Hong Kong officials played down the affair as simply a language mix-up between Hong Kong border guards and PLA troops.
